units.filledPassage:
A college tasting club compared tea prepared from the same batch of dried leaves. The plant material was placed in water, but the resulting drink was not simply the original material in a smaller shape. Some substances could dissolve, entering the water at a molecular level, while many solid pieces remained visible.

The club called the prepared drink an infusion because water had stood in contact with the plant material to extract soluble substances. To remove floating pieces before tasting, the students poured it through a filter. This step separated larger solids; it did not necessarily remove the substances already present in solution.

They kept the water temperature the same across samples, measuring how hot it was when each preparation began. They also recorded the volume of water in each cup, since adding the same amount of leaf material to different quantities of water could produce different results. The time in contact with water was the variable they deliberately changed.

A stronger concentration meant that more of the relevant dissolved material was present per unit of drink. It did not mean that every flavour became more pleasant. A long steep could taste bitter, with an unpleasant sharp quality for some participants. Individual preference was recorded separately from preparation time.

The students described the smell rising from each cup as its aroma. Solid material remaining after pouring was the residue. They kept smell, taste and leftover solids as separate observations. Their small comparison could describe these particular preparations, but it could not establish one perfect brewing time for every tea, cup or drinker.

units.filledPassage:
A walking club invited a shoe fitter to a preparation meeting. Several members assumed that the printed size alone would establish comfort. The fitter measured each foot's length from back to front, then checked its width from side to side. Two feet with a similar first measurement could still require differently shaped shoes.

The back part of the foot was the heel. It needed to remain reasonably secure rather than rise excessively with every step. The fitter adjusted the laces, the cords threaded through the upper part of the shoe, to alter how it held the foot. Pulling harder was not always better: a shoe that became too tight could squeeze the wearer.

The bottom part contacting the ground was the sole. For the intended walk, it needed to bend appropriately rather than behave like an entirely stiff board. A suitably flexible material could accommodate that movement. This did not establish that the softest possible shoe was suitable for every surface.

The group also discussed friction, rubbing between surfaces that could irritate skin during repeated steps. Concentrated pressure meant force acting over a limited area, another possible source of discomfort. These mechanisms were related but were not identical descriptions.

A small fluid-filled skin injury caused by repeated rubbing was a blister. Members were advised to stop and seek suitable help if discomfort developed, rather than treat pain as proof that a shoe was becoming effective. The meeting was about checking fit before the walk; it did not provide a diagnosis or claim that one shoe design could prevent every foot problem.

units.filledPassage:
An orchard class watched bees moving among apple flowers. The bright outer flower parts were petals. Their colour, together with the flower's scent, could contribute to attracting visitors. The class kept visual appearance separate from the smell perceived near the blossoms.

Bees collected nectar, a sugary liquid, as one food resource. Fine grains of pollen could also attach to their bodies. These grains had a role in plant reproduction and were not another name for the sweet liquid. A visit could therefore involve food collection while also moving reproductive material.

The receiving flower part was the stigma. When suitable pollen reached it, the movement was described as pollination. This event did not itself guarantee that every flower would eventually develop into a mature apple. Later conditions and processes still mattered.

Researchers could transfer pollen deliberately between flowers in a controlled comparison. They covered some blossoms to reduce visits by insects, the animal group that includes bees. The coverings were part of an experiment, not an assertion that all plants relied on bees or that no other movement of pollen was possible.

An apple was the eventual fruit considered in this example, while the observation period was seasonal because flowering occurred during a particular part of the year. The class recorded flower visits and later development separately. Counting one bee landing was not the same as counting one apple produced. This distinction helped pupils ask what their observation actually measured before drawing conclusions about the orchard's harvest.

units.filledPassage:
A rail museum used a stationary carriage to explain boarding arrangements. The vehicle did not move during the demonstration. Visitors compared its floor with the platform, noticing that two different dimensions could cause difficulty.

The horizontal distance was the separation across from platform edge to vehicle doorway. The vertical difference concerned how far one surface stood above the other. Reducing one did not automatically remove the other. A narrow space could still include a significant step.

Where both surfaces were at the same height, the guide described them as level. A remaining gap could still lie between them. A short flat board could bridge that space under the museum's controlled demonstration, forming a connection rather than changing the height of the whole platform.

A sloping ramp could accommodate a height change. Its gradient described the steepness of the slope, so the distance available for the slope mattered. The demonstration did not suggest that every steep board was an appropriate boarding aid.

The staff used a portable device that could be carried into position and removed after use. Correct alignment meant that its relevant edges and the doorway were placed in the intended relation. The guide checked this before anyone used the model.

The exhibit distinguished a building feature, a vehicle position and a movable aid. It did not offer instructions for independent use on an active railway. Its purpose was to show why calling a station accessible required more information than saying that one step had been removed. Conditions at the actual door and platform mattered together.

units.filledPassage:
A conservation seminar examined repeated surveys of ponds for an amphibian. The relevant habitat was the wetland environment used by the species. Whether a site was actually occupied during the defined study period was its occupancy state. The observation process was a separate matter: a present animal could remain unnoticed.

The probability of recording the species when it was present concerned detection. Search duration, weather and observer experience could affect that process. The team recorded survey effort as time spent searching, rather than assuming every visit represented the same opportunity to notice an animal.

A written protocol specified how each visit should be conducted. Following it improved comparability, although it could not make imperfect observation disappear. Additional visits provided temporal replicates, repeated observations of the same site within the period for which the occupancy state was assumed stable. The team explicitly considered whether that stability assumption was defensible.

Measured features used to explain variation were covariates in the statistical model. Some described sites; others described visits. Treating them as interchangeable would confuse ecological conditions with observation conditions. The model combined these components to estimate the probability that sites were occupied, rather than simply equating an empty notebook with an empty pond.

Conclusions remained uncertain where observations were limited or the assumptions were weak. The investigators reported that uncertainty rather than rounding every result to certainty. A claim of local extinction, the disappearance of the species from a site, would require more justification than one unsuccessful search.

The exercise did not assert that repeated visits inevitably identified every hidden state. It showed why absence of a record and absence of an organism were different propositions. Assumptions about changes during the study and relationships among visits had to be evaluated alongside the numerical output.

units.filledPassage:
A neighbourhood time bank allowed members to provide approved services and earn credits measured in hours. The arrangement encouraged reciprocity, a pattern of mutual giving and receiving, without requiring the person who received one service to repay the same provider directly. It was distinct from an ordinary cash wage for employment: the scheme's credits did not claim to settle every legal question about work.

When a member completed an accepted task, the recorded service was a contribution to the scheme. A coordinator checked that both parties agreed the task had occurred. An entry became verified after that confirmation, rather than merely because one participant had submitted a request.

Transactions were kept in a ledger, a chronological accounting record. A member's available balance reflected credits earned and used under the local rules. Recording the same task twice would distort that amount even if the duplicated descriptions were individually plausible.

Using earned credits to receive a service was redemption. The scheme's ability to meet such requests depended on willing members and suitable skills; a positive account did not guarantee immediate access to every kind of assistance. The coordinators therefore distinguished a record from a promise of unlimited supply.

The rules defined eligibility, the conditions under which a person could join and participate. They also specified an expiry date after which unused credits would no longer remain valid. That condition was explained before members joined, rather than introduced after their contributions.

If participants disagreed about a recorded task, a dispute could be submitted for review. The review considered the evidence and the announced rules; it did not assume that the larger recorded balance necessarily belonged to the more truthful person. The seminar used the example to separate social purpose, accounting events and obligations. Calling the arrangement mutual aid did not remove the need to explain what each account entry meant.

Unused: 责任相关但本段没有定义负债数额或特定承担义务，工资/资格不能以它替换。

A statistics office prepared a table showing counts of service users across small districts. Several cells contained very few people. Publishing an exact count beside a distinctive category could make information about an individual easier to discover, so the underlying records were treated as confidential rather than open for unrestricted inspection.

The office's rule used a threshold, a numerical cutoff below which a cell required additional protection. Removing the displayed value was suppression. Yet hiding a single cell did not necessarily protect it: row and column margins could allow a reader to subtract all visible counts and recover the missing one.

The analyst therefore considered complementary protection, withholding further cells so that the first hidden value could not be obtained by that simple subtraction. This was a coordinated treatment of the table, not an assertion that every unprinted number was equally sensitive.

Another approach used rounding, reporting counts to a stated numerical interval rather than retaining all their digits. A different technique deliberately added controlled changes, or perturbation, to the published values. These methods affected what readers could calculate, and their properties depended on the specified procedure.

The agency assessed utility, the usefulness of the published table for its intended analyses, alongside disclosure risk. Combining categories through aggregation could reduce detail, but it might also conceal differences important to users. A larger table was therefore not automatically more informative for every purpose.

Before public release, the office tested whether protected values could still be derived from combinations of totals and earlier publications. It documented the transformations and limitations. The exercise showed that a visible blank was a presentation feature, whereas protection concerned what could be learned from the entire information environment. No single visual treatment guaranteed that all routes to identification had disappeared.

A seminar prepared a critical edition of a short historical poem surviving in several handwritten copies. The copies were textual witnesses: material sources that preserved forms of the work, not necessarily independent testimonies to its original wording. A later copy might have been made directly from an earlier one.

Comparing readings across the copies was collation. The comparison revealed a variant where one manuscript used a different word from another. Frequency alone did not settle which reading should enter the edited text, since several copies could share a single copying history.

The edition recorded alternatives in an apparatus, a structured set of notes documenting textual differences and editorial decisions. Readers could inspect those notes instead of having to accept a smooth printed line as an unqualified reproduction of every source.

A physical loss that left part of the poem missing was a lacuna. If an editor proposed wording unsupported by a surviving source to fill that space, the proposal was a conjecture. Its plausibility did not turn it into newly discovered manuscript evidence. Such proposals were explicitly marked.

To emend the text was to correct a suspected error through an announced editorial intervention. The team distinguished that action from a transcription, a written rendering of what a particular source actually showed. A carefully prepared rendering could preserve a reading that the editor considered mistaken.

A diplomatic presentation followed the source's written features closely under stated conventions. It had a different purpose from an edition that silently regularised spelling for convenient reading. Neither format was automatically suitable for every research question.

Finally, the team recorded provenance, the documented origin and custody history of each manuscript. That history could inform evaluation, but it did not guarantee an error-free text. The seminar's governing principle was transparency about the route from material sources to editorial claims. A readable final poem and a demonstrable account of its production were related achievements, not interchangeable ones.
